turns.prompt_text: I filled this bernzomatic torch up with lighter fluid. Is there any way I can ameliorate my mistake? Attached 1 file. - f0709dbb-5f05-422f-ba68-7f6d3eef4c5f
turns.response_html:
That is definitely a situation where we want to move quickly but carefully. Most Bernzomatic micro-torches (like the ST2200 or similar models) are designed to run exclusively on butane gas, not liquid lighter fluid (naphtha).

Filling a pressurized butane reservoir with liquid fuel can damage the seals, clog the internal burner, or create a serious fire hazard when you try to ignite it.

Immediate Steps to Take

  • Do Not Ignite It: Under no circumstances should you try to click the starter. Liquid lighter fluid doesn't vaporize the same way butane does; it could leak or flare up uncontrollably.
  • Work in a Well-Ventilated Area: Go outside or to a garage with the door open to avoid inhaling fumes.
  • Empty the Reservoir: * Invert the torch over a safe container (like a metal tray or an old glass jar).
    • Depress the fill valve on the bottom using a small screwdriver or a specialized tool.
    • Allow all the liquid to drain out. Caution: Be gentle with the valve to avoid damaging the needle or the rubber O-ring.

The "Amelioration" Process

Once you have drained the liquid, the goal is to remove the oily residue left behind by the lighter fluid:

  1. Evaporation: Leave the torch with the fill valve depressed (you can sometimes wedge it open safely, though holding it is safer) for several hours or overnight in a well-ventilated spot. Since lighter fluid is more oily than butane, it takes much longer to evaporate.
  2. The "Flush" (Optional but Recommended): If you have a can of butane, you can try to "flush" the system. Inject a small amount of butane, let it sit for a minute, and then bleed it out through the fill valve again. The butane acts as a solvent to help carry out any remaining liquid fuel.
  3. Check the Seals: Lighter fluid can cause the rubber gaskets meant for butane to swell or degrade. After it has dried completely, refill it with proper butane and check for any hissing sounds (leaks).

The Reality Check

If the torch feels "sticky" inside or the flame is sputtering/producing yellow soot after you refill it with butane, the internal wick or catalyst may be contaminated beyond repair. Given that these micro-torches are precision tools, it’s often safer to replace the unit if it doesn't return to a clean blue flame immediately.

turns.prompt_text: Okay so this bernzomatic has been sitting here for a month or two now If I try to lite it it doesn't work
turns.response_html:
Since it's been sitting with liquid fuel inside for a month or two, the lighter fluid has likely done one of two things: it has either completely degraded the rubber seals inside the valve mechanism, or it has saturated the internal expansion chamber and burner nozzle with oily, unvaporized residue.

Because butane torches rely on the fuel instantly vaporizing from a liquid into a gas before it hits the spark, the heavy, oily nature of lighter fluid completely chokes the system.

Here is how to determine if it's salvageable or if it's time to call it a loss:

1. The Purge Test

Before throwing it out, you need to clear the lines completely.

  • Go outside to a safe, open area.
  • Take a small screwdriver or a pen and depress the fill valve on the bottom of the torch.
  • What to look for: Does liquid lighter fluid still squirt out, or does nothing happen at all?

2. The Diagnosis

  • If liquid fluid comes out: The torch is flooded with the wrong fuel. You can try to hold the valve down until it's completely empty, let it sit open in the sun for a few hours to evaporate the remaining residue, and then refill it with high-quality butane.
  • If nothing comes out, but it won't light: The internal jets are clogged with dried lighter fluid residue, or the internal seals have failed. When you press the ignition trigger, do you hear a faint hissing sound of gas escaping? If you hear absolutely nothing when the gas wheel is turned up, the path is entirely blocked.

The Verdict

Honestly, given that the liquid fuel has had weeks to sit against the delicate internal O-rings and micro-nozzles, the internal components are likely ruined. These micro-torches aren't designed to be completely disassembled down to the internal valves for cleaning.

If a thorough purge and a fresh fill of proper butane gas doesn't get it hissing and sparking a clean blue flame, it’s best to safely dispose of it and replace it. Trying to force a clogged or compromised torch to light can lead to unexpected flares if the valve suddenly gives way.

turns.prompt_text: So my other option here is I would like to take it apart and disassemble it entirely for educational purposes
turns.response_html:
Taking it apart for educational purposes is a great way to see how the venturi effect, piezo igniters, and gas valves work firsthand. Since the torch is already compromised, it makes a perfect teardown subject.

Before you grab the screwdrivers, you just need to ensure the unit is entirely safe to handle.

The Safety Protocol

Even though it isn't lighting, there could still be a pocket of pressurized fuel or liquid trapped inside the tank.

  1. Purge the Tank: Go outside and use a small tool to completely depress the fill valve on the bottom until you no longer hear any hissing or see any liquid escaping.
  2. Leave the Valve Open: Turn the flame adjustment wheel all the way to maximum and click the continuous lock on (if it has one) to ensure any internal pathways are wide open to the air.

What You'll Find Inside

Once the housing screws are removed (usually small Phillips or Torx screws hidden under the rubber grip or stickers), the torch typically splits into a few distinct modular systems:

  • The Piezo Igniter: This is the little spring-loaded plastic block with a wire coming out of it. When you click the trigger, a tiny internal hammer strikes a quartz crystal, generating a high-voltage electrical pulse (around 10–20 kV) that jumps a gap at the nozzle tip to create the spark. You can take this module out entirely—it operates mechanically without any gas.
  • The Venturi Brass Nozzle: Follow the gas tube to the tip. You'll see a brass piece with tiny air intake holes. This is the venturi tube, designed to mix atmospheric oxygen with the high-velocity gas to create a hot, efficient blue flame rather than a lazy yellow one.
  • The Gas Regulator and Valve Assembly: This connects the main fuel tank to the nozzle line. You'll be able to see how the dial physically restricts or opens the fuel path, and you'll likely spot the degraded or swollen rubber O-rings that caused the torch to fail after its encounter with the lighter fluid.

Enjoy the teardown, watch out for the sharp edges of any internal clips, and have fun exploring the mechanics behind it!
